title: Why the floor
hookLine: in langar people sit in rows on the floor, everyone level, whoever they are
last: KIRTAN SOHILA — THE HOME FILLS UP.

lines: LONG STRIPS OF CLOTH ON THE FLOOR.
cards: In a restaurant, look at the chairs. The booth by the window. The stool at the bar.
The high chair for the baby. The corner table where the owner seats his friends. Chairs sort us: by money, by age, by who we know.
Now take the chairs away. All of them. Put long strips of cloth on the floor, in straight lines, and ask everyone who walks in to sit on them, cross-legged, shoulder to shoulder.
The man who owns six restaurants sits there. So does the man who washes their dishes. You met this picture on day two.

teach.b: Pangat. A row, a line of people sitting together to eat. In langar, it's the long line on the floor, side by side, everyone served the same food.

teach.h: FIRST THE PANGAT, THEN THE SANGAT.
teach.b: You met a saying on day fifty-one: first the pangat, then the sangat. Tradition says Guru Amar Das asked everyone who came to see him to sit and eat in the row first, whoever they were.
The story goes that even the emperor Akbar sat on the floor and ate before he met the Guru. Why the floor? Because it's the one place where no one can be higher.
A chair can be taller, a table can be at the front, a seat can be closer to the kitchen.

teach.h: ON THE FLOOR, NO ONE IS HIGHER.
teach.b: But the floor is the floor. It's humble in a physical way too: it's hard to feel grand with your knees folded under you and a plate in your hands. And the row has no head; no end of the line counts more than the other.
The Guru Granth Sahib has a line that Sikhs connect with this.
Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase, that all are sharers in God's grace, and no one is seen to be outside it.
The pangat puts that on the ground where you can see it. In recent decades, some gurdwaras abroad argued bitterly over tables and chairs in the langar hall, and the Akal Takht ruled for the floor.
Today some gurdwaras keep the floor and also set chairs aside for elders and anyone who can't sit down low. The row still holds.

how: In langar halls people traditionally sit on the floor in long rows, the pangat, and are served the same food by volunteers; some gurdwaras also provide chairs for elders and those who cannot sit on the floor.

practice: If you can, sit on the floor, cross-legged or however is comfortable; if you can't, sink a little lower in your seat and feel the ground under you.

Picture a long row stretching out on both sides, filled with real people: someone you admire, someone you find difficult, someone you've never met. Everybody at the same height, waiting for the same food.

wordCard.voice: Pangat. The row: people sitting side by side on the floor in langar, everyone level, whoever they are.
